q: my social media feeds have suddenly exploded with parenting content: what to buy, product reviews, how to hold, feed, or soothe a baby, tummy time tips and endless advice. Most of these ads and posts are clearly targeted at mothers
cx: At 16 weeks, after a few searches on baby supplies, her feeds fill with ads and advice aimed at mothers.

q: I’m already exhausted by my social algorithms and I'm actively trying to reset them by browsing in incognito mode.
cx: Same 16-week mother, worn out by targeted pregnancy content, browsing incognito to escape it.

q: I opened a few links for baby brands that a friend sent me and suddenly my Instagram is covered by feeding suggestions and TikTok is full of moms ranting about very difficult situations that I'd really prefer not to watch 😅 he looked for some practical topics and got nothing.
cx: She compares her ad-flooded feeds with her partner's, which show nothing after his practical searches.

q: the father and I are constantly discussing these things but he is mostly focusing on the bureaucratic side (parental leave, childcare options, medical appointments, etc.).
cx: How the couple splits pregnancy preparation: she gets the baby-supplies content, he handles leave and paperwork.

q: had told MIL that my partner and I had spent $3000 on new garden furniture but that we have bought nothing for the baby and that we are totally unprepared.
cx: A partner's relative complained to the mother-in-law that the couple had bought nothing for the baby.

q: we have everything but a stroller and grocery items (formula and nappies). I’m only 23 weeks so I have plenty of time!
cx: At 23 weeks she lists what is still left to buy and feels she has time.

q: I fear this may get worse when the baby comes and that I will have to spend a lot of mental energy navigating how to set boundaries with her.
cx: She expects a judgmental in-law relative to become a boundary problem once the baby arrives.

q: I’ve spent seven months curating this registry for things I want and need. And she still doesn’t know what to get and told my sister she will just give me money.
cx: Her own mother says the 100-item registry leaves her not knowing what to get.

q: I have bought all the big ticket items off Facebook or on sale, with a several hand me downs from my sister, so everything on the registry is pretty inexpensive.
cx: How she bought big items second-hand and kept the registry cheap.

q: She’s complained to my sister that she didn’t like how I announced it to her and she’s mad that I might not have visitors right away.
cx: Her mother objects to a no-visitors-at-first plan for after the birth.

q: This pregnancy has been TOUGH. I was really struggling the first 20 weeks. And it took me way too long to realize this wasn't just hard on me and my body.. it's been hard on my husband too.   I've just been completely checked out.
cx: At 34 weeks, a first-time mother wants to give her husband a gift after a hard pregnancy.

q: we just bought a house, we're first time parents, and we're not rich by any means.
cx: Budget context for choosing an affordable keepsake gift for her husband.

q: I’m scared about losing our life here, scared about becoming a father, scared about my wife’s mental health, scared about my own mental health, and scared that despite everything I’m trying to do, I’m still not doing enough.
cx: A husband on a work visa loses his job as his wife nears the third trimester.

q: Maybe advice on how to support a pregnant partner who is struggling emotionally without losing yourself in the process.
cx: Same husband asks how to support his pregnant wife without losing himself.

q: That has completely changed how my wife had been imagining her birth and postpartum experience. She had envisioned having the baby here, building her career here, and having a certain kind of support system.
cx: His job loss and a possible move abroad upend his wife's picture of birth and support.

q: She states that she would resent me if I didn’t use the full 3 months of PFML for her after birth.
cx: An expectant father must split 12 weeks of paid leave between his own surgery and the birth.

q: she told me “you’re gonna do whatever you want anyway but I’ll never forgive you if you do that”
cx: His wife's reply when he proposed splitting the leave between surgery and the newborn weeks.

q: This is our OB, and could well be the person who delivers our baby. From my standpoint, my trust in her is completely shattered.
cx: After a medication mix-up at the 36-week visit, a husband loses trust in the OB who may deliver.

q: She says "if this happened to me, I would say 'oh well.'"
cx: The OB's response when the husband raised the injection error.

q: I think she would be nervous starting from zero somewhere else, since we've done the hospital tour, it's very close by, etc.
cx: Why the couple stays at the same practice at 36 weeks despite losing trust.

q: when I go to check in with the client at least 24 hrs after the birth, they do not respond. I don’t want to be pushy but get the sense that they just want me for the birth which is fine.
cx: An on-call hospital-programme doula finds clients ignore her check-ins after the birth.

q: they recently started a poll with the whole family to take bets on when shes born. The person closets to the date and time wins a giftcard......
cx: At 38 weeks, her in-laws run a family betting pool on the birth date.

q: I am worried then my frustration is only going to get worse once baby comes as they will want access to her but I will also be in a fragile state of recovery.
cx: She fears in-laws wanting access to the newborn while she recovers.

q: I told my inlaws we may need some help a few mornings/evenings and they were so excited to help and proceeded to ask if we had a place for my FIL to take his naps, and a place to accommodate their dog crate, etc....
cx: Her request for postpartum help turns into in-laws needing to be hosted.

q: We recently purchased a house and moved (would not suggest at 38 weeks but thats how life unfolded).
cx: Moving house at 38 weeks, helped by her own parents.

q: In the past he's used both of our money to buy things like a pram or cot without having my input at all and it's so frustrating the way he acts like he's the only one having this child.
cx: At 19 weeks, after a baby-name row, she recalls her boyfriend buying big items without her.

q: when he ordered the pram and stuff without me she actually shouted at him for it and he cancelled the order before it could arrive.
cx: His mother made him cancel a pram order placed without the expecting mother.

q: A few months before the due date, I hit up a local EMT for a crash course in pediatric first aid. I'm SO glad we did that. I don't think I learned anything new, but it was a huge boost in confidence
cx: A father's list of what helped: a home first-aid session arranged through the local fire department.

q: We opted out of having any sort of midwife / doula. If we could go back, we'd probably reconsider.
cx: Looking back after a complicated delivery, a father regrets having no doula.

q: it would have been nice to have someone in the room whose sole focus was to make sure we were getting what we needed, even if it was just the play by play of what was happening.
cx: What he wanted in the room when staff stopped explaining during the delivery.

q: prepare for the onslaught of ads about shit that you "need.” Do your due diligence on car seats, strollers, and the high chair, when the time comes. The rest? Meh. You probably don't need it.
cx: A father's verdict on baby purchases after the newborn months.

q: I'm convinced that everyone who tells you stuff like "soak it all up, enjoy it while you can, etc." doesn't remember what holding a baby that can't support its own head was like.
cx: On what people said to them after coming home with the newborn.

q: I did feel like some family members just wanted to come in to snag a photo of being the “excited [relative]” and then bounce.
cx: Family support mostly helped, but some visitors came for photos and left.

q: I found that breastfeeding culture kind of stunk. It was a ton of pressure and we didn't always appreciate how nurses/doctors/etc. handled it.
cx: A father on the feeding pressure the couple felt from staff after the birth.
